overview: This card follows the atlas record called “Yemen,” but that single label hides several different political maps. Its 1920 to 1938 shape misses Sana’a and much of the northern highlands as well as British Aden and Socotra; later shapes add the highlands but still omit Aden and Socotra. In history, an independent northern imamate/kingdom emerged after Ottoman rule, a northern republic began in 1962, and the British-ruled south became independent in 1967. The two sovereign states united on 22 May 1990 as the Republic of Yemen. The atlas has no geometry after 2020, while the continuing republic has long been divided by war and rival de facto administrations. Treat the outline as a navigation aid, not a legal border or a claim about who controls each place.

periods.title: A northern imamate and a British-ruled south
periods.summary: After Ottoman rule ended, an independent imamate and later Mutawakkilite Kingdom governed much of northern Yemen, while Britain ruled Aden and protectorates in the south.

periods.title: Northern revolution and civil war
periods.summary: The Yemen Arab Republic was proclaimed in the north in 1962, beginning a civil war with regional intervention and a United Nations observation mission.

periods.title: Two independent Yemens
periods.summary: The north continued as the Yemen Arab Republic; the south won independence in 1967 and took the name People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen in 1970.

periods.title: Unification, elections and a civil war
periods.summary: North and south formed the Republic of Yemen on 22 May 1990. A 1994 southern secession attempt failed, and later political transition did not resolve regional and institutional disputes.

periods.title: War and divided de facto rule
periods.summary: Houthi forces seized Sana’a in 2014; a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 at the internationally recognized government’s request. Rival authorities and fragmented institutions persisted in 2026.

sections.title: How one atlas label became a united republic

items.text: The atlas begins this record in 1920, but there was no single state covering its modern-looking label then. Much of the north was ruled by an imamate that later used the name Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen. Britain controlled Aden and protectorates in the south. This is why a map reader should not project the 1990 republic backward over everybody living inside today’s borders.

A revolution proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic in the north in September 1962. Fighting between republicans and royalists quickly drew in Egypt and Saudi Arabia; the United Nations created an observation mission in 1963. A “republic” on paper therefore did not mean that stable nationwide government arrived overnight.

Southern Yemen became independent from Britain on 30 November 1967 and was renamed the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen in 1970. For more than two decades, the Yemen Arab Republic in the north and the southern republic were separate sovereign states, each with its own government and international relationships.

The two governments signed a unification agreement in Sana’a on 22 April 1990, and it entered into force on 22 May. In its authentic Arabic, the new state is named «الجمهورية اليمنية» (al-Jumhūriyya al-Yamaniyya), “the Republic of Yemen.” Arabic is written from right to left; this is a real legal phrase, not decorative pseudo-script.

Unification did not settle every struggle over power and resources. The transition included power-sharing and a 1993 election, then collapsed into war in 1994. Southern leaders declared secession, but no state recognized it; northern forces captured Aden in July, and the Republic of Yemen legally remained one state while postwar rule became more centralized.

Houthi forces and allies seized Sana’a in September 2014. President Hadi later moved to Aden, and a Saudi-led coalition began military operations on 26 March 2015 at his request. The United Nations has continued mediation, but a negotiated nationwide settlement had not restored unified administration by 2026.

Control today needs a date attached. A World Bank project document prepared in January 2026 described a Sana’a-based Houthi authority and an Aden-based internationally recognized government, with duplicated institutions, currencies and rules. A UN statement on 30 January 2026 likewise referred to “Houthi de facto authorities” in Sana’a-controlled areas and the internationally recognized government in Marib. These descriptions report control; they do not create a new international border.

sections.title: Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature

items.text: Old Sana’a sits about 2,200 metres above sea level. Its decorated multi-storey tower houses, dense lanes, mosques and green bustans were shaped over centuries with local stone, fired brick and earth. Fun fact: from a rooftop, the city can look like a gingerbread skyline dusted with white icing, but the white patterns are carefully worked architectural decoration, not frosting.

Shibam’s mud-brick towers rise as high as seven storeys inside a compact walled plan, which is why it is often nicknamed a desert “skyscraper city.” The towers are brilliant climate-and-space engineering, but mud walls need constant care. UNESCO also warns that modern water supplies without equally good drainage have harmed buildings and sanitation, a reminder that adding taps without planning where wastewater goes can backfire.

Zabid was a major centre of Islamic learning, with mosques, madrasas and an old university embedded in a market town of shaded streets and courtyard houses. Courtyards helped families combine airflow, household work and privacy. This scholarly and architectural heritage predates the modern Republic of Yemen; preserving it is a modern responsibility, not evidence that today’s state built it.

Socotra’s isolation produced an extraordinary living laboratory: UNESCO records 825 plant species, of which 307, about 37 per cent, occur nowhere else. The umbrella-shaped dragon’s blood tree is the celebrity, but the whole archipelago matters. Biodiversity evolved over deep time, so it is not a government “invention”; conservation is the achievement people can choose now.

A small UNDP-backed experiment trained women and young people to install and manage solar microgrids in three frontline communities. UNDP reported that local electricity costs fell by 65 per cent and that women became technicians and business managers. That is clever, practical wartime problem-solving, but three communities are a pilot, not proof that Yemen’s national power crisis has been solved.

sections.title: Families, neighbours and going to school

items.text: Family and neighbourhood life varies enormously among highland cities, coastal towns, islands, farms and displacement camps. Historic courtyard houses could screen domestic life from a busy street, while Shibam’s vertical homes stacked rooms upward inside a tight city wall. Architecture gives clues about privacy and social life, but it cannot tell us that every family lived, or lives, the same way.

In Jader village, children once walked about an hour to a distant school and crossed a dangerous road. Parents and neighbours helped establish a closer learning space; UNICEF supported a new school. The story shows how education can be a family logistics puzzle as much as a classroom lesson. In 2025 UNICEF estimated 3.7 million children aged 5 to 17 were out of school nationwide.

Bathrooms can decide whether a child stays in class. Mohamed, a student with diabetes, used to carry a 1.5-litre bottle because his school lacked safe water and usable toilets. Girls sometimes went home or avoided drinking because there was no privacy. After repairs brought running water and separate facilities, school became easier. In 2017 UNICEF-supported work improved WASH facilities in 232 schools, substantial, but far from every school.

In displacement sites in Al Jawf, some women and children collected water by donkey, missed lessons and had to use open ground as a toilet. Emergency water points and latrines improved privacy and cleanliness. Kid fact with a serious point: a toilet is a small room with a huge job, it protects dignity, school attendance and drinking water all at once.

sections.title: Medicine, clean water and public health

items.text: Community midwives often connect remote families to the health system. In Marib, midwife Warda provided antenatal and postnatal checks, health education and family-planning counselling, and arranged referral when care was beyond what she could safely handle. Her story shows skilled local care and quick judgment; it does not mean every village has a trained midwife or a functioning referral route.

At Habil Jabr clinic in 2025, families brought children for vaccines, vitamins and treatment of fever and other common illnesses. UNICEF reported supplying 288 primary-health-care kits to supported facilities in late 2024 and early 2025. Kits keep routine care moving, but they cannot repair an entire health system, pay every worker or end shortages caused by war.

Vaccination teams achieved an important but limited result in southern governorates: WHO reported in March 2026 that transmission of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 had been interrupted there, supported by vaccination and surveillance training. “In the south” matters. It would be wrong to turn this into a claim that all polio risk had disappeared throughout Yemen.

Clean-water lessons can be lifesaving science. In 2024, 6,448 pupils at 20 schools in Lahj learned why handwashing matters and how open defecation, uncovered wells and contaminated water can spread cholera and other disease. The funniest bathroom lesson may be the truest: germs do not care whether a toilet topic feels embarrassing, so asking good questions beats pretending toilets do not exist.

The emergency remained severe on 24 September 2026. WHO reported that about 60 per cent of assessed health units were fully functioning, and only 6 per cent offered trauma care, amid new displacement and disease outbreaks. These are dated operational figures, not a permanent description of Yemen. They explain why small successes, one stocked clinic, repaired toilet or trained vaccinator, matter so much.

ending.text: The Republic of Yemen has not “ended.” It remains the single internationally recognized UN member created by the 1990 merger, while rival authorities exercise de facto control over different areas and war has fragmented institutions. The atlas stops drawing the country after 2020 because its basemap coverage stops, not because Yemen vanished. As of 24 September 2026, conflict and humanitarian need were still changing conditions on the ground, so any present-control description should be read with its date attached.
